Prefix-cache eviction is a critical memory management mechanism primarily utilized in modern Large Language Model (LLM) inference engines, such as vLLM or TGI, to optimize the generation process via Key-Value (KV) caching. To understand eviction, one must first grasp the role of the KV cache. During autoregressive text generation, a transformer model computes attention keys and values for every token in the context. Recalculating these for every new token generated is computationally expensive, so systems store the KV vectors of previous tokens in GPU memory. A "prefix" refers to a contiguous sequence of tokens at the beginning of a prompt (e.g., system instructions or multi-shot examples). If multiple requests share the same prefix, the KV cache for that prefix can be reused, saving significant computation time. However, GPU VRAM is finite. Prefix-cache eviction is the strategic process of removing these stored KV blocks from memory when space is needed for new, active requests, ensuring the system remains responsive without crashing due to out-of-memory (OOM) errors.
